title: Tell them apart: differences or ratios?
summary: Decide whether a table or graph shows linear or exponential growth by checking what stays constant over equal steps.
prereqText: You need arithmetic, percentages, and plotting points on axes. If percentages feel rusty, review "percent change" before lesson 2.

blocks.html:
Two apps both have 5 thousand users today, and both add users every week. A friend says "they are growing the same way." Here are their first five weeks. Both columns increase, so what could "the same way" even mean, and how would you check it?

week      0   1   2   3   4
App A     5   8  11  14  17   (thousands of users)
App B     5  10  20  40  80   (thousands of users)

blocks.purpose: Show that equal steps in x add the same height for a linear table and multiply the height for an exponential table.
blocks.alt: A chart of weeks 0 to 4 on the horizontal axis and users in thousands on the vertical axis. App A rises as a straight line from 5 to 17, about 3 more each week. App B starts at 5 as well but climbs ever more steeply, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, doubling each week and overtaking App A before week 2.

blocks.prompt: A table (illustrative data) gives y = 3, 6, 12, 24 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3. If the pattern continues with equal steps in x, what is y at x = 5?

feedback.0: 36 comes from adding the last difference (12) once. But the differences here are 3, 6, 12: they are not constant, so "keep adding" is the wrong rule.
feedback.1: 48 is y at x = 4, one step too early. Check: x = 4 is 24 × 2 = 48, and x = 5 is 48 × 2.
feedback.3: 60 comes from adding 12 twice to 24 (a linear continuation). The values are doubling, not growing by a fixed amount.

blocks.explanation: The ratios are 6/3 = 2, 12/6 = 2, 24/12 = 2: each step multiplies by 2. So x = 4 gives 48 and x = 5 gives 96.

blocks.instructions: For each table, decide first and only then read the feedback. Compute both the differences (new − old) and the ratios (new ÷ old) on paper if you are unsure. All x values step by 1, starting at 0. All data are invented for practice.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed that "increasing" does not decide anything: every table here rises except the decays. What decides is which quantity is constant. The squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) are the trap: their differences grow, so they look exponential, but their ratios keep shrinking, so neither test is satisfied. "Neither" is a legitimate answer.

items.feedback: Ratios: 2, 2, 2, 2. Constant ratio means exponential. The differences 3, 6, 12, 24 grow.
Differences 3, 5, 7, 9 are not constant; ratios 4, 2.25, 1.78, 1.56 are not constant either.
Ratios are all 0.5, so it is exponential, here decaying because the factor is below 1.
Ratios are all 1.1 (growth of 10% per step). The differences 0.7, 0.77, 0.847 grow slowly, which is easy to miss.
Differences are all −5. Linear can decrease too.

config.debrief: Constant difference gives linear and constant ratio gives exponential. If neither holds, neither model fits.

blocks.title: Two kinds of "constant"
blocks.html:
Take a table where the input x goes up by the same step each row. Two questions sort most tables:

  • Is the difference constant? Compute new − old for each pair of neighbouring rows. If they all agree, the output changes by the same amount over equal steps: linear growth. The shared number is the common difference.
  • Is the ratio constant? Compute new ÷ old for each pair. If they all agree, the output changes by the same percentage over equal steps: exponential growth. The shared number is the common ratio or growth factor.

This is how the textbook separates the two: linear growth adds the same amount over equal steps of the input, exponential growth increases by the same percentage [1]. Its first comparison pairs 2^x (outputs 1, 2, 4, 8, … 64) with 2x (0, 2, 4, … 12) and concludes that exponential growth soon dwarfs linear growth [1].

Why ratios matter when differences look "almost constant". A 10% rise on 7 is 0.7, but 10% of the new value 7.7 is 0.77: a constant percentage means a growing amount. That is why you need the ratio test, not just a glance at the differences.

Rows must be equally spaced in x. If x jumps from 2 to 4, one row covers two steps. Divide by the number of steps (for a ratio, take a root, or just insert the missing row) before comparing.

Simplification: a finite table can only be consistent with a pattern. Four matching ratios do not prove the next value; they make the model worth testing.

blocks.title: Reading a graph
blocks.html:
On a graph, apply the same two tests to equally spaced x positions:

  • A straight line adds the same height for each step to the right: constant difference, linear. A line has the same steepness everywhere.
  • An exponential graph with b > 1 curves upward and keeps getting steeper; with 0 < b < 1 it falls steeply, then flattens toward zero. Either way, the height at x + 1 is a fixed multiple of the height at x. Its y-intercept is the initial value, and the x-axis (y = 0) is a horizontal asymptote that the graph approaches but never reaches [1].

So to decide from a graph, read the height at three or four equally spaced x values and then compute differences and ratios just as you would for a table. Judging by the "look" alone is risky: over a short window, an exponential with a factor close to 1 looks almost straight.
Think of two staircases. In a linear staircase every step rises the same height. In an exponential staircase every step is a fixed multiple of the one before, so each riser is taller than the last.
blocks.limits: The staircase picture suggests exponential means "gets steeper". That holds only when the factor is above 1. With a factor between 0 and 1 the risers shrink and the curve flattens. A factor very close to 1 also makes the first steps almost identical to a linear staircase.

blocks.title: Worked example: classify a table
blocks.html:
x   0   1    2    3     4
y   2   6   18   54   162

steps.html: x goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: equal steps of 1, so neighbouring rows can be compared directly.
6 − 2 = 4, 18 − 6 = 12, 54 − 18 = 36, 162 − 54 = 108. The differences are 4, 12, 36, 108, not constant, so the table is not linear.

steps.prompt: Test the ratios. What do you predict?
steps.html: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 18 ÷ 6 = 3, 54 ÷ 18 = 3, 162 ÷ 54 = 3. The ratio is a constant 3, so the table is consistent with exponential growth with common ratio 3. Notice also that the differences themselves are multiplied by 3 each time (4, 12, 36, 108).

steps.prompt: State the conclusion with its evidence and its limit.
steps.html: "Exponential: the ratio is 3 at all four steps, while the differences are not constant. The first value is 2, so I would expect y = 486 at x = 5, if the pattern holds." The prediction is an extrapolation and rests on only five points.

blocks.task: Invented data: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y = 5, 6.5, 8.45, 10.985. (a) Compute the three differences and three ratios. (b) Decide the model. (c) Predict y at x = 4.
hints: Subtract each value from the next one, then divide each value by the previous one.
Do the three differences agree? Do the three ratios agree?
If the ratio is r, then the next value is the last value times r.
rubric: I computed both differences and ratios, not just one
I stated which one is constant and what it equals
My prediction uses the constant I found
blocks.solution: Differences: 1.5, 1.95, 2.535 (not constant). Ratios: 6.5/5 = 1.3, 8.45/6.5 = 1.3, 10.985/8.45 = 1.3 (constant). So the data are consistent with exponential growth, factor 1.3 (30% per step). At x = 4: 10.985 × 1.3 = 14.2805.

blocks.task: Invented data, both tables for x = 0, 1, 2, 3 (equal steps): Table P: 20, 26, 32, 38. Table Q: 20, 26, 33.8, 43.94. They agree at x = 0 and x = 1. Decide each model with evidence and give each table's value at x = 5. Then say which is larger at x = 5 and how you could have guessed that without computing.
rubric: Explains that Q multiplies, so its steps get bigger
blocks.solution: P: differences 6, 6, 6, so linear, P(4) = 44 and P(5) = 50. Q: ratios 1.3, 1.3, 1.3, so exponential, Q(4) = 57.122 and Q(5) = 74.2586. Q is larger: both start with a rise of 6, but Q's rise is multiplied by 1.3 each step while P's stays 6.

blocks.html: Four questions. Your first attempt is recorded as performance; later attempts are practice.

questions.prompt: Invented data: x = 0, 1, 2, 4 and y = 3, 6, 12, 48. Which statement is best?
options: Exponential: the factor is 2 per one-unit step (from x = 2 to x = 4 is two steps and 12 → 48 is × 4 = 2 × 2)
Linear: every difference is a multiple of 3
Impossible to tell without a graph

feedback.0: The differences are not constant, but the x gaps are unequal, so you cannot compare rows directly. Account for the step size first.
feedback.2: Differences that are all multiples of 3 are not constant differences. Linear requires the same amount per equal step.
feedback.3: A graph is not required: dividing by the number of steps (or filling in x = 3) lets the table decide.

questions.explanation: The row for x = 4 covers two steps. Per one-unit step the factor is 2 (since 2 × 2 = 4). The ratios per equal step are then 2, 2, 2.

questions.prompt: Invented data: y = 12, 18, 27 at x = 0, 1, 2. What is the common ratio?
questions.feedbackWrong: Divide each value by the one before it (new ÷ old); do not subtract.

questions.prompt: Heights read from a graph at x = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 2, 3, 4.5, 6.75 (illustrative). What is the best conclusion?
options: Exponential: each height is 1.5 times the previous one
Neither, because the heights are not whole numbers

feedback.0: "Rises steadily" is not a test. The differences 1, 1.5, 2.25 are increasing.
feedback.2: Whole numbers are not required for either model.
feedback.3: Differences of 1, 1.5, 2.25 are growing by a factor of 1.5; they are not constant.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why is "the values keep increasing" not enough to say that a table is exponential?
rubric: Gives or implies an increasing linear example
Names the constant ratio (or constant percentage) as the real test
Mentions that some increasing tables are neither
questions.model: Linear tables also increase. For example 5, 8, 11, 14 increases by a constant 3. A table is exponential only if the ratio between neighbouring rows is constant. Some tables increase and are neither, such as 1, 4, 9, 16.

blocks.task: New context, invented data. Monthly active users in millions: App P: 1.0, 1.4, 1.8, 2.2 (months 0 to 3). App Q: 1.0, 1.2, 1.44, 1.728. A colleague says "Q grew less than P every month so Q is the slower app and will stay behind." (1) Classify each app with numbers. (2) Explain what is wrong with the colleague's reasoning. (3) Estimate each app's users at month 12 if its pattern held, and say whether you trust that estimate.
rubric: P: constant difference 0.4; Q: constant ratio 1.2
Points out that comparing early increases ignores that Q multiplies
Month 12: P about 5.8 and Q about 8.9 million
States that extrapolating 12 months from 4 points is uncertain
blocks.model: P: differences 0.4, 0.4, 0.4, so linear: P(12) = 1 + 0.4 × 12 = 5.8 million. Q: ratios 1.2, 1.2, 1.2, so exponential: Q(12) = 1.212 ≈ 8.92 million. The colleague compares only the early increases. P adds 0.4 forever, but Q's increase is 20% of a growing total (0.2, 0.24, 0.288, …) and passes 0.4 within a few months. Q is slower early and faster later. The month-12 numbers extrapolate from four points; a real app's growth rate can change, so treat them as a model's consequence, not a forecast.

blocks.prompt: Write the two questions you will ask of any table before naming a model. Then write one situation where you would still not be sure after asking them.
